newsitem.title: USA: Dollar posts new eight-week high versus yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar posts new eight-week high versus yen.

text.p: The dollar rose above 110 yen for the first time in nearly two months on Wednesday, fanned by remarks from a Japanese Finance Ministry official and speculation that low Japanese interest rates will continue to prompt investors to favour the dollar.
Eisuke Sakakibara, director general the Ministry's International Finance Bureau told reporters that Japan has no specific target for the dollar/yen rate.

"It's a continuation of the prospects of no Japanese rate hike in the near future, Sakakibara's comment and break of the psychological 110 yen level; those three things are what's getting us through," said Bill Marr, foreign exchange manager at Credit Commercial de France.
The dollar rose to 110.35 yen -- its highest since July 15 -- up from 109.85 yen late Tuesday.
Against the German mark, the dollar was unchanged at 1.5110 marks after a three-day stretch of gains culminated early Wednesday at 1.5155, the highest dollar level since July 16.

Sakakibara -- "dubbed Mr. Yen" by the market -- is the architect of Japan's 1995 offshore investment deregulation package, which many consider the catalyst for the dollar's rise from its historic low under 80 yen last year.

Sakakibara seemed to refute comments by another economic official who suggested Japan preferred a 105-to-110 yen range for the dollar, and his comments dovetailed with those of U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who reiterated his support for a strong dollar to reporters late Wednesday.

The yen's slide against the dollar was also fuelled by ongoing speculation that Japan's weak economy and recent bankruptcies in Japan's financial community have killed any chance of higher Japanese interest rates soon.
At the same time, U.S. interest rates are expected to rise soon, increasing the incentive for investors to switch from low-yielding Japanese deposits to more attractive dollar investments.
"Interest rate differentials are in favour of the dollar and the differentials are going to increase," said Tom Sharpe, assistant manager of foreign exchange at Sakura Bank.
Traders have been buying dollars in expectation that the Fed would boost short-term interest rates when its policy makers meet on Sept. 24.
U.S. inflation data later in the week may receive extra scrutiny following Federal Reserve Governor Janet Yellen's comment Tuesday that the U.S. economy was in an "inflationary danger zone."
Surprisingly strong inflation data often leads to adverse movements and great volatility in currency, bond and stock markets, leaving traders wary of holding positions ahead of a report.
"There is no question people are probably looking to take profits ahead of inflation figures in the U.S.," said Stephen Flanagan, vice president at Credit Agricole.
Wall Street economists expect the government to report Thursday that August producer prices rose one-tenth of 1 percent and look for a two-tenths of a percent gain in consumer prices on Friday.
In other trading, the dollar was stable at 1.2355 Swiss and it rose to Canadian $1.3715 from C$1.3705 on Tuesday.
